chapter_theme: One song at Thiruvadanai (திருவாடனை): the diseased body dies, is wailed over, carried on a bier and burned to ash before it stinks, and the poet asks not to seek such a birth again; the praise names Siva who drank the poison, before whom Murugan taught the Agama of knowledge.

981.reading: The poet follows the flesh-filled, sickly body to its end: when life goes the townsfolk gather and wail until they tire, lay it on a bier, carry it off before it stinks, and set it in the fire without shame until it is ash; he asks for grace so that he will not seek this birth again. The praise names Vishnu who dances on the serpent's hood, Brahma on the flower, the gods and the eight mountains, saved when Siva ate the halahala as nectar, and Murugan who, before that Siva, gave the Jnana Agama with right conduct and devotion, at Adanai.
981.nuance: நாணாமல் வைத்துவிட: the kin burn the body 'without shame', with no more regard than for refuse. The remedy is not the body's improvement but an end of birth (இப்பிறவி நாடாது). ஆசார பத்தியுடன் ஞானாகமத்தை அருள் makes Murugan the teacher of the Agama to Siva, the Om story in another dress.

links.note: Both follow the corpse from the wailing and the drums to the fire; the Naladiyar ends with the dying carrying the dead, 981 with the ash and a prayer not to be born again.

981 follows the dead body: the townsfolk gather and wail till they tire (ஊரார் குவித்து ... அழுதோய), carry it before it stinks and set it in the fire till it is ash, and asks not to seek this birth again. Tirumular has the whole town gather and wail (ஊரெலாம் கூடி ஒலிக்க அழுதிட்டு), call him a corpse, burn him and bathe and forget. The scene is the same step by step; Tirumular ends with the mourners' forgetting, the song with a prayer against rebirth.
